messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Call Center Agent
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 39

She is 60, a South Eastern Asian woman who has been married for more than three decades, and she still measures time by the morning her younger brother died. Before that day, her life feels ordinary to her when she talks about it: early coffee with her husband, long shifts as a call center agent, careful budgeting, weekend calls with relatives scattered across different countries. She describes herself then as practical and patient, someone used to calming upset strangers over the phone and keeping her own feelings neatly folded away until there was time for them.

Her brother lives back in their home country. They are close in the way siblings can be when they have survived immigration, family obligations, and distance together. She sends money when he needs it, reminds him to take his medication, and teases him for forgetting birthdays. The call comes unexpectedly, just before she is due to leave for work. An aunt is crying so hard she can barely speak. There has been an accident. At first she cannot understand the words. Then she understands all at once. She remembers dropping the mug in her hand and watching coffee spread across the kitchen floor while her husband keeps saying her name.

What disturbs her most is how quickly the world continues. Her headset is still hanging by the door. The bus still arrives. Customers still call to complain about passwords and billing errors while, on the other side of the world, her brother’s body is being prepared for burial. She is unable to travel in time for the funeral. The distance becomes part of the trauma itself. She watches the service through a shaky phone video, held by a cousin who keeps lowering the camera. She sees only fragments: shoes on dusty ground, the corner of a white cloth, relatives’ voices breaking apart in static. For months afterward, those broken images replay in her mind without warning.

At work, she tries to return quickly because she does not know what else to do. She has spent years being the calm voice on the line, but now ordinary calls feel strangely threatening. When a customer raises his voice, her chest tightens as if she is back in that first phone call, bracing for terrible news. Sometimes the beep in her headset before a new call makes her jump. She starts dreading the ring of her personal phone too. Late at night, if it lights up unexpectedly, she feels a bolt of panic before she even looks at the screen. She tells herself it is irrational, but her body does not listen.

Sleep becomes unreliable. She falls asleep from exhaustion, then wakes at 2 or 3 a.m. with her heart pounding. In some dreams her brother is alive and calling for her; in others she is the one trying to reach him, dialing again and again while the line stays dead. She gets out of bed so she will not wake her husband, and sits in the kitchen in the dark, scrolling through old voice messages she has saved from him. She listens to them repeatedly, both comforted and undone by the sound of his ordinary, living voice.

Her husband notices that she is not the same. She is more irritable, especially when he asks gentle questions she experiences as pressure. Their children tell her to rest, but she hears herself snapping at them and then feels ashamed. She avoids family gatherings where people might mention her brother, yet she also feels wounded when no one mentions him at all. On the anniversary of his death, she cooks his favorite dishes and cries quietly while washing the plates. She cannot bear to delete his number from her phone. She also cannot bear to call it.

Over time, her world narrows. She used to enjoy video calls with relatives overseas, but now she postpones them because seeing familiar faces brings back the helplessness of not being there. News reports about accidents or sudden deaths catch her attention and stay with her for hours. She has become watchful, as though catastrophe is always approaching by telephone. At the call center, coworkers know her as dependable, but she now keeps to herself during breaks. It takes effort to sound warm and composed for customers. By the end of a shift, she feels wrung out, her shoulders hard with tension.

What troubles her is not only the grief, but the sense that part of her remains frozen in that kitchen, coffee on the floor, phone pressed to her ear, waiting for the next unbearable sentence. She says she misses her brother every day. More quietly, she says she misses the version of herself who could answer a ringing phone without fear.
